text: Want to see how India has kept time for thousands of years? Let's go.
Up in the sky, two great clocks are always ticking: Surya, the Sun, and me.
The Sun's clock gives us the year and its seasons. My clock gives us the month, as I wax and wane.
Most calendars you use today watch only the Sun.
But the Hindu calendar is lunisolar. It watches both of us at once.
Try the switch below to compare them.
The almanac that tracks our two clocks is called the Panchang.
Pancha means five, and anga means limb. So Panchang means five limbs of time.
Tithi, the lunar day. Vara, the weekday. Nakshatra, my star mansion. Yoga, and Karana.
Together, they describe any moment. Tap a petal to peek inside.
Tithi is the heart of the Panchang.
Picture the Sun and me lined up together. That's Amavasya, the new moon.
Each day I race ahead. Every time I gain twelve more degrees on the Sun, one tithi is complete.
Fifteen tithis as I grow brighter: Shukla Paksha, the bright half, ending at Purnima, the full moon.
Then fifteen more as I fade: Krishna Paksha, the dark half, back to Amavasya.
But my orbit is an ellipse, not a circle. Close to Earth I speed up; far away I slow down.
So a tithi follows my real speed each day. It can last anywhere from about twenty to twenty-six hours.
Go ahead. Drag me around my orbit.
Vara is the weekday. Seven days, named after the seven grahas you can see with your own eyes.
Ravi the Sun, Soma the Moon, Mangala, Budha, Guru, Shukra, and Shani.
Watched from Earth, each takes its own time to circle the sky. Shani needs about twenty-nine and a half years. I need just twenty-seven days.
Line them up from slowest to fastest. Each of the day's twenty-four horas, or hours, is ruled by the next one in line, so each new day starts three steps along.
Follow those steps and a seven-pointed star appears, giving the order of the week.
One more thing: the Hindu day begins at sunrise, not at midnight.
Why only seven days? Because the ancient astronomers tracked what they could see.
The Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn all shine to the naked eye. Uranus and Neptune need a telescope, so they were never counted.
In Sanskrit these bodies are called grahas: those that grasp, or influence. Jyotisha counts nine of them, the Navagraha.
The last two are Rahu and Ketu. My path is tilted against the Sun's path, and they are the two points where the paths cross.
When the Sun and I meet at one of these points, an eclipse happens. The graha seems to grasp the light.
Rahu and Ketu are chhaya grahas, shadow planets. With no body and no light to mark a day, they get no weekday, and the week keeps seven.
Now look beyond us, at the fixed stars.
Ancient astronomers divided my path into twenty-seven nakshatras, or lunar mansions.
Each spans thirteen degrees and twenty minutes, and I spend about a day in each.
Every name means something. Rohini, the red one, is the star Aldebaran. Krittika, the cutter, is the Pleiades. Chitra, the bright one, is Spica.
The nakshatra I'm in when you are born becomes your birth star.
Tap any star group to meet it, and hear its name.
Add the Sun's longitude to mine, and cut the circle into twenty-seven parts of thirteen degrees twenty minutes. That gives twenty-seven yogas.
Each yoga has a name and a character. Harshana means joy, and Siddhi means success. Both are welcomed for new beginnings.
Others, like Vyatipata and Vaidhriti, are traditionally a time to pause.
Tradition links yoga with space, Akasha, and with health, mood and relationships. Slide me to explore.
Karana is half a tithi: just six degrees of my lead over the Sun.
So every tithi has two karanas, and a lunar month has sixty.
There are eleven karanas. Seven movable ones, Bava to Vishti, repeat eight times.
Four fixed ones, Shakuni, Chatushpada, Naga and Kimstughna, appear once, around the new moon.
Tradition links karana with earth, Prithvi, and with action. Vishti, also called Bhadra, is usually avoided for new beginnings.
Here's how Yoga and Karana compare.
Twelve lunar months make a year.
Each month is named after the nakshatra where the full moon shines. A full moon near Chitra gives Chaitra. Near Vishakha, Vaishakha.
Meanwhile, the Sun walks through twelve rashis. The moment it enters a new one is a Sankranti.
When does a month begin? In the South and West, including Karnataka, a month runs from new moon to new moon. That's Amanta.
In the North, it runs from full moon to full moon: Purnimanta. So the same day can carry two month names!
Here's a puzzle. Twelve of my months add up to about three hundred and fifty-four days.
The solar year is about three hundred and sixty-five. So we fall eleven days short, every single year.
Left alone, festivals would drift backwards through the seasons.
So when a lunar month passes with no Sankranti at all, it becomes an extra month: Adhika Masa.
That happens about once every thirty-two and a half months. 2026 itself had an Adhika Jyeshtha.
Years are counted in eras. 2026 is Vikram Samvat 2083, and Shaka Samvat 1948.
And festivals follow the Panchang. Ugadi is Chaitra Shukla Pratipada. Holi is Phalguna Purnima. Diwali falls on the new moon of autumn.
But Makar Sankranti follows the Sun into Makara, so it stays near January fourteenth, every year.
Now you know why Diwali moves, and Sankranti doesn't.
Now it's your turn. Find the Panchang for any day. Maybe your birthday?
Or keep going with the optional deep dives. Namaste, and see you in the sky!
This deep dive explores how tradition explains the number five.
A Western calendar tracks the date. In the traditional view, the Panchang tracks the quality of time, whether a moment supports or resists what you do.
Each limb is linked with one of the five great elements, the Pancha Mahabhutas.
Vara is fire, Agni: the physical vitality of the day. Tithi is water, Jala: emotions and relationships.
Nakshatra is air, Vayu: the mood of the mind. Yoga is space, Akasha: the bond that holds the day together. And Karana is earth, Prithvi: action and results.
Think of them as five coordinates, a GPS for time. Leave one out, and tradition says the moment has a blind spot.
The astronomy behind each limb is exact. The meanings are the tradition's interpretation. Tap a limb to switch it off.
Three rulers measure the same circle: twelve rashis, twenty-seven nakshatras, and a hundred and eight padas.
Each rashi spans thirty degrees. Each nakshatra spans thirteen degrees twenty minutes, split into four padas of three degrees twenty minutes.
So every rashi holds exactly nine padas, or two and a quarter nakshatras. Nakshatra and rashi borders meet only three times: at Ashwini, Magha and Mula.
Each rashi has a ruling graha and an element: fire, earth, air or water. And each pada has a sound, traditionally used to choose the first syllable of a baby's name.
Tap the wheel to explore, or look up your own birth star in the finder.
Here's how astronomers, ancient and modern, measure the sky.
Imagine the sky as a giant sphere around Earth. Every star sits at a fixed spot on it.
The Sun's yearly path across this sphere is the ecliptic, Kranti Vritta. Rashis and nakshatras are marked along it, and all the grahas wander close to it.
Earth's equator, projected onto the sky, makes the celestial equator. It's tilted twenty-three and a half degrees to the ecliptic, and that tilt gives us the seasons.

Positions are measured as longitude: degrees along the ecliptic from a zero point. The Western zodiac starts at the spring equinox. The Indian zodiac starts from the fixed stars, at the start of Ashwini, opposite Chitra.
So a graha's rashi and nakshatra is simply the slice of sky behind it, measured along the ecliptic, like segments of an orange.
Tap a graha in the list to fly to it. Use the controls below to change the date, run time, or stand on Earth.
Every measurement in the Panchang is an angle, seen from Earth.
Stretch out your arm. Your little finger covers about one degree. Three fingers, about five. A fist, about ten.
The Moon's disc is only half a degree wide, yet it travels about thirteen degrees a day, a little more than one fist.
Twelve degrees of lead over the Sun makes one tithi. Tap any two objects to measure the angle between them.
The fixed stars aren't quite as still as they seem, from where we watch.
Earth's axis wobbles slowly, like a spinning top, tracing a full circle about once every twenty-six thousand years.
This is precession. It moves the equinox backwards against the stars, about one degree every seventy-two years.
Around 285 CE the two zodiacs matched. Since then they have drifted about twenty-four degrees apart. That gap is the ayanamsa.
It even changes the pole star. Today it's Polaris, which Indian tradition calls Dhruva. Around the year 14,000, it will be Vega.
And it's why Makar Sankranti, on January fourteenth, now comes about three weeks after the winter solstice. Drag the years to see it.
Finally, let's step outside, under the sky at the place and date set in the finder below.
The dark ground is your horizon. The glowing band is the ecliptic, with the rashis and nakshatras along it.
The rashi rising in the east is the lagna, the ascendant. It changes about every two hours.
Find me, and the grahas. Drag to look around, run time forwards, or step outside to see your horizon from above.
Rahu and Ketu aren't bodies at all. They're two points in the sky.
My orbit is tilted about five degrees to the Sun's path. The two places where my path crosses it are the nodes: Rahu, where I cross going north, and Ketu, where I cross going south.
Most months I pass a little above or below the Sun, so nothing happens. But when a new or full moon falls near a node, the three of us line up.
At Amavasya near a node, I cover the Sun: a solar eclipse. At Purnima near a node, I slip into Earth's shadow: a lunar eclipse.
That's the story of Rahu and Ketu swallowing the Sun and Moon. They're chhaya grahas, shadow planets, because they mark exactly where the shadows fall.
The nodes slide backwards around the zodiac once every eighteen point six years, about eighteen months in each rashi. That's why they are always shown moving backwards.
And the equinoxes? They're the same kind of crossing: where the Sun's path meets Earth's equator. Rahu and Ketu are to my path what the equinoxes are to the Sun's.
Run time forwards to watch eclipse seasons come and go, or tap an eclipse in the list to jump to it.
The Sun hand and the Moon hand race around the zodiac. The Moon laps the Sun about once a month.
The angle between them is the phase. Each twelve degrees of it is one tithi, and each six degrees is a karana.
Add the two positions instead of subtracting them, and you get the yoga. It runs a little faster, about fourteen degrees a day.
In the charts below, each rising line is a phase clock. When the Moon speeds up, the tithi steps get shorter.
Play, pause, change the speed, or tap the charts to jump in time.
Here is time, told the Indian way.
The day starts at sunrise and is divided into sixty ghatis of twenty-four minutes. Each ghati has sixty palas, and each pala sixty vipalas.
The outer ring glows for daylight. Day and night are each split into four praharas, or watches.
Around the dial, the Panchang fills in: the year in Vikram Samvat, the masa, the paksha, tithi, vara, nakshatra, yoga and karana.
It's live and ticking. Change the date, time or place below to read any moment.
How long is a month for me? It depends on what you measure against.
Against the fixed stars, I go once around the sky, through all twenty-seven nakshatras, in about twenty-seven and a third days. That's the sidereal month.
But from new moon to new moon takes about twenty-nine and a half days. That's the synodic month, the one the tithis and the lunar months follow.
Why the difference? While I circle Earth, Earth is also travelling around the Sun, about twenty-seven degrees in that time.
So when I'm back in front of the same star, the Sun has moved on. I need about two more days to catch up and line up with it again.
Watch the two bars: the star bar fills first, and the new moon bar a couple of days later.
